title: He Came Through Qualifying and Saved Four Match Points. Then the Top Seed Was Out.
excerpt: Rounak Chouhan, 18, ranked 80th in the world, stunned tournament No. 1 seed Chou Tien Chen in straight games to lead India's surge at the US Open badminton in Fullerton, California.
body:
When Rounak Chouhan arrived in Fullerton, California, for the US Open badminton tournament, he did not even have a place in the main draw. The 18-year-old from India, ranked 80th in the world, had to fight through qualifying rounds just to earn the right to step onto the same court as the top seed.

On Thursday, he did considerably more than that.

Chouhan produced the upset of the tournament, beating World No. 6 and men's singles top seed Chou Tien Chen of Chinese Taipei 21-17, 26-24 in straight games to advance to the quarterfinals. The match lasted 49 minutes. It felt longer than that — because in the second game, Chouhan had to save four match points before converting his own second match point to close it out.

## A Pattern of Six-Point Storms

The scoreline tells only part of the story. In both games, Chouhan fell behind — and in both, he produced identical six-point surges to turn things around.

In the first game, Chou led 17-15 and appeared to be heading toward a routine hold. Chouhan then won six consecutive points to steal the game 21-17. In the second, Chou was in an even more commanding position at 17-11. Again, Chouhan found six straight points from somewhere. The game went to deuce, then past it, with Chouhan saving four game points in the 24-24 stretch before sealing the win on his second opportunity.

The man he beat is no club player having a bad day. Chou Tien Chen is 36 years old, a former World No. 2, a World Championship bronze medallist, and one of the most decorated players in Chinese Taipei's badminton history. His career record entering the US Open stood at more than 540 wins. He had beaten his way past Yu-Kai Wang in the Round of 32 just the day before, looking characteristically composed.

## From Qualifiers to the Last Eight

Chouhan's path to this point was not smooth. He began in the qualifiers, beating France's Enogat Roy 21-19, 21-16, then came from a set down to defeat Chinese Taipei's Kuo Kuan Lin 13-21, 21-14, 21-10. In the main draw's first round, he had to navigate an all-Indian clash against S. Sankar Muthusamy — a former World Junior Championships silver medallist — winning a tight 23-21, 21-16 encounter.

Chouhan is not entirely unknown in junior circles. He was part of India's bronze medal-winning team at the BWF World Junior Mixed Team Championships in Guwahati last year, where India earned a historic first medal in the mixed-team event before falling to defending champions Indonesia in the semifinals. Now he is making his mark on the senior circuit, and doing it on American soil.

He will face Israel's Misha Zilberman in the quarterfinals.

## India's Broader Takeover in California

Chouhan's result was the headline act, but India's dominance at the US Open extended well beyond one upset. Kidambi Srikanth, the experienced former World No. 1 and 2021 World Championship silver medallist, capped the day with a comprehensive 21-14, 21-13 victory over Malaysia's Lee Zii Jia — a former All England champion and a player ranked significantly higher than Srikanth. It was the kind of surgical performance that suggested Srikanth still has plenty of high-level badminton left in him.

In the women's singles, three Indian players reached the quarterfinals. Tanvi Sharma, a World Junior Championship silver medallist and fifth seed here, dispatched Chinese Taipei's Tung Ciou-Tong 21-12, 21-19. Rakshitha Sree routed Chen Su Yu of Chinese Taipei 21-4, 21-19, while sixth seed Devika Sihag beat Thailand's Tonrug Saeheng 21-17, 21-19.

The tournament is being held at Fullerton, in Orange County — an area with one of the largest Indian-American communities in Southern California. The BWF World Championships are scheduled for New Delhi later this year, and a strong US Open showing serves notice that India's next generation is ready for the home crowd.

## What the Diaspora Is Watching

For Indian-Americans in Southern California, the US Open has delivered something rare: world-class Indian badminton within driving distance. The tournament in Fullerton runs through the weekend, with the quarterfinals, semifinals, and finals still to come.

The combination of Chouhan's fairytale run, Srikanth's ruthless dispatching of a former All England champion, and three Indian women in the last eight makes this the strongest Indian showing at a BWF Super 300 event on American soil. With the BWF World Championships headed to New Delhi's Indira Gandhi Stadium later this year, these results suggest India will have more than just home support to rely on when the biggest stage arrives.
